fields.caption:
A design system does not start with buttons, cards, or components.

It starts with the invisible rules that make every screen feel consistent.

Before building components, define your:

Color system
Typography scale
Spacing system
Grid and layout
Elevation and effects
Motion principles
Icons and illustrations
Design tokens

These foundations help designers make faster decisions, developers build with fewer inconsistencies, and products scale without becoming messy.

Components are only the output.

The foundation is the real system.

Save this carousel before building your next design system.

Which foundation do you usually define first?

concepts: Design Principles: High-level guidelines that define how a product should feel and act as filters for design decisions.
Design Tokens: The smallest, atomic pieces of a design system (colors, spacing, radius) that translate design decisions into code variables.
Typography Scale: A consistent set of font sizes and properties that ensure predictable and readable text across a product.
Spacing System: A defined set of spacing values used for margins, padding, and layout to ensure visual consistency.
Motion System: Standardized durations and easing curves that define how elements move and change within the interface.
fields.summary: A guide on the foundational elements required to build a robust design system, emphasizing that principles, tokens, and scales should be established before creating UI components.
tips: Build the foundation before building components.
Use design principles to resolve design debates.
Create color roles (e.g., primary, success, error) instead of random color values.
Ensure all spacing, margins, and padding snap to a defined grid.
Keep layouts invisible by standardizing columns and breakpoints.
Use design tokens to bridge the gap between design and code.
Maintain a consistent icon style and illustration language to define product personality.
fields.transcript: [slide 1] VAMSHI.WORK 1/10 FOUNDATIONS OF A DESIGN SYSTEM. Before buttons. Before cards. Before components. Build the foundation first. [slide 2] VAMSHI.WORK 2/10 WHY FOUNDATIONS MATTER. Most design systems fail because teams start with components. But components are only the surface. The real system starts with: rules, scales, tokens, principles. Foundations create consistency. Components simply inherit it. [slide 3] VAMSHI.WORK 3/10 DESIGN PRINCIPLES. Before creating UI... Define how your product should feel. Clear over clever, Accessible by default, Fast to scan, Consistent everywhere, Mobile first. Principles become decision filters. When design debates happen, principles decide. [slide 4] VAMSHI.WORK 4/10 COLOR SYSTEM. Don't create random colors. Create roles. Examples: Primary, Secondary, Success, Warning, Error, Surface, Border, Text. Then create shades: 50 -> 100 -> 200 -> 900. [slide 5] VAMSHI.WORK 5/10 TYPOGRAPHY SCALE. Typography should feel predictable. Define: Font families, Font weights, Font sizes, Line heights, Letter spacing. Example scale: 12, 14, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48. A system scales. A collection doesn't. [slide 6] VAMSHI.WORK 6/10 SPACING SYSTEM. Most inconsistency comes from spacing. Use a spacing scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64. Everything snaps to the grid. Margins, Padding, Layouts, Components. Consistency becomes automatic. [slide 7] VAMSHI.WORK 7/10 GRID & LAYOUT. A design system needs layout rules. Define: Columns, Gutters, Margins, Breakpoints, Container widths. Examples: Mobile -> 4 columns, Tablet -> 8 columns, Desktop -> 12 columns. Good layouts feel invisible. [slide 8] VAMSHI.WORK 8/10 ELEVATION & EFFECTS. Depth needs rules too. Define: Shadow levels, Blur values, Radius scale, Borders, Opacity tokens. Example: Elevation 1, 2, 3, 4. Without rules... everything floats differently. [slide 9] VAMSHI.WORK 9/10 MOTION SYSTEM. Motion is part of the product language. Define: Duration, Easing, Delays, Enter animations, Exit animations. Example: Fast -> 150ms, Normal -> 250ms, Slow -> 400ms. Good motion explains change. Bad motion distracts. [slide 10] VAMSHI.WORK 10/10 ICONS & ILLUSTRATIONS. Visual language should stay consistent. Define: Icon style, Stroke width, Corner radius, Filled vs outline, Illustration style. One icon style. One illustration language. One product personality. [slide 11] VAMSHI.WORK 11/12 DESIGN TOKENS. This is where everything connects. Tokens translate design into code. Examples: Primary Blue -> color.primary.500, 16px -> spacing.md, 8px radius -> radius.sm. Tokens make scaling possible. Without tokens, design systems break. [slide 12] VAMSHI.WORK 12/12 COMPONENTS ARE NOT THE BEGINNING OF A DESIGN SYSTEM. They are the result of a strong foundation. Build the rules first. Build the UI second. FOUNDATIONS FIRST. COMPONENTS SECOND.
workflow_steps: Define design principles to act as decision filters.
Establish a color system based on roles rather than random colors.
Create a typography scale for predictable text sizing.
Implement a spacing system using a defined scale that snaps to a grid.
Set layout rules including columns, gutters, and breakpoints.
Define elevation and effect rules for depth.
Establish a motion system for duration and easing.
Standardize icons and illustrations for visual consistency.
Translate design foundations into code using design tokens.

fields.caption:
Rebuilding my design workflow with @paper.design 

This is how I went from scattered assets to an organized brand system any agent can recognize and work with. 

For context: I’m currently building an app for my journaling brand and I’ve made hundreds of design iterations scattered across different platforms over the past years. 

Instead of guessing or starting from scratch, I gathered the assets that felt closest to where the brand is now, and used them to build the brand guidelines my design agents will refer to throughout the build.

The workflow:

1. Paste the most relevant assets into Paper, straight from Figma
Super straight forward. Copy, paste, done.

2. Frame the assets in Paper and copy the link

Everything in Paper is HTML/CSS, so the frame becomes real context an agent can read with accuracy.

3. Hand the link to Claude Code

 Prompt I used:
 “Hey, I just gathered these assets at this link: [link]. Can you take a look and create a brand guideline? Color system, icons and assets, typography, spacing, components, and anything you notice to be a recurring theme.”

4. Refine manually

Back and forth between design agent, Paper and manually tweaking things.

5. Turning this into design tokens so every project stays consistent.

Will cover this in the next vid.

—

About Paper: 

Been using Paper for a few months now, I was playing around this new agentic workflow, and see how it can help me bring my digital projects to life. I just love the back and forth flow, from prompting to designing and shipping to production.

Next vid: creating design tokens.
